title: International Grapes: Recognition and Style
description: A practical path to identify key international grapes and connect aroma, structure, and origin.

lessons.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
lessons.intro: Cabernet Sauvignon is the benchmark for structured reds: tannin, longevity, and precision.
lessons.final: You can now connect Cabernet Sauvignon to structure, climate, and aging potential.

slides.title: Varietal identity
paragraphs: Cabernet Sauvignon comes from Cabernet Franc crossed with Sauvignon Blanc.
Its thick skins and high tannin make it naturally suitable for long aging.

slides.title: From climate to glass
paragraphs: Cooler sites often show herbaceous tones and tighter fruit.
Warmer sites usually show riper black fruit and higher alcohol.

lessons.title: Merlot
lessons.intro: Merlot teaches roundness: softer tannin, rich fruit, and major blending value.
lessons.final: You now understand why Merlot is key for balance and drinkability.

slides.title: Taste profile
paragraphs: Merlot often brings plum-like fruit and smooth texture.
Compared with Cabernet Sauvignon, it is usually less austere on the palate.

slides.title: Role in blends
paragraphs: In many blends, Merlot helps round out stricter varieties.
Didactically, it is useful to understand how one grape changes total perception.

lessons.title: Pinot Noir
lessons.intro: Pinot Noir teaches finesse: gentle extraction and high sensitivity to place and climate.
lessons.final: You can now recognize signals of elegance, delicacy, and terroir transparency.

slides.title: Sensitive grape
paragraphs: Pinot Noir has thin skins and needs precision in both vineyard and cellar.
It usually gives lighter color and finer tannin than many international reds.

slides.title: Sensory reading
paragraphs: Red fruit, floral tones, and subtle spice are common references.
It is excellent for training attention to detail in tasting.

lessons.title: Chardonnay
lessons.intro: Chardonnay is perfect for understanding how climate and winemaking shape style.
lessons.final: You can now distinguish fresher Chardonnay from richer, oak-influenced expressions.

slides.title: Versatility
paragraphs: It can produce lean and crisp wines, or broad and creamy ones.
Harvest timing, fermentation, and aging strongly influence final profile.

slides.title: Style deduction
paragraphs: Steel tends to preserve freshness and pure fruit.
Oak and lees work can increase volume and spicy/buttery complexity.

lessons.title: Sauvignon Blanc
lessons.intro: Sauvignon Blanc trains the nose: herbaceous, citrus, or tropical tones depending on climate.
lessons.final: You have reinforced the link between aromatic profile and production area.

slides.title: Aromatic signature
paragraphs: In cooler regions it often shows grass, tomato leaf, and citrus.
In warmer regions it can move toward tropical fruit and softer tension.

slides.title: Didactic use
paragraphs: It is one of the best grapes for aroma-recognition exercises.
Comparing it with Chardonnay is a classic training drill.

lessons.title: Riesling
lessons.intro: Riesling means precision: high acidity, aromatic clarity, and strong aging potential.
lessons.final: You can now read freshness, residual sugar balance, and evolution potential in Riesling.

slides.title: Acidity and balance
paragraphs: Riesling often keeps high acidity even at full ripeness.
This allows dry, off-dry, or sweet styles without losing energy.

slides.title: Evolution
paragraphs: With time, Riesling can gain complexity while keeping drive.
Didactically, it is perfect for understanding acidity and longevity.
